turns.text:
I need to vent and then I need a plan. Thursday night our biggest prospect ever, a hospital network, sent a final offer: $480k a year, which roughly doubles our revenue. It lapsed at 10 the next morning and a competitor was in the final round. I called Tom twice and texted him. Nothing. He went dark the one night it mattered. Friday morning I spent two and a half hours on the phone with the hospital, got the timeline pushed from ten weeks to fourteen, and got an extension clause on top. Then I signed. We have nine months of runway. I wasn't going to let it walk.

Tom calls me at 10, says I committed his team without him, and hangs up on me. An hour and a half later he posts in the engineering channel that we "did not agree" to the timeline and tells everyone not to start. In front of the whole team. He has sandbagged most of what I've brought him this year because of his migration, which is now five months late. I think he wants the migration as his excuse to never touch the sales side. I'm exhausted from carrying this company by myself.

Our founders' meeting is Monday at 9. How do I handle Monday?

That's a lot to carry into a weekend. You landed the biggest deal the company has ever had, under a hard deadline, on nine months of runway. You couldn't reach your cofounder. You spent the morning negotiating the timeline from ten weeks to fourteen. Then your reward was being hung up on and publicly countermanded in front of the team. Feeling exhausted and alone in carrying this makes sense.

**What your account shows, and what it leaves open**

Some of this is solid ground for you:
- You tried to reach Tom: two calls and a text before a 10am deadline.
- You didn't just accept their terms. You pushed the timeline out by 40% and added an extension clause, which protects his team.
- A hung-up call and a public "don't start" post mean the conflict is now in front of the team. That's a fair thing to be upset about, and the team needs a clear answer about what they're doing.

Other parts I can't settle from one side:
- What Tom's night looked like and why he didn't respond.
- Whether fourteen weeks is actually feasible given what his team is carrying. He may know things about capacity you don't, or he may not.
- Whether you two have an understanding, spoken or assumed, about committing engineering timelines. If he believes you broke one, he'll experience this very differently than you do.
- Whether "sandbagging" and "wanting the migration as an excuse" describe what's happening. That's your read after a hard year, and it may be part of it. But if you say it Monday, he'll hear an accusation, and the meeting will be about that instead of the deal.

**For Monday**

Two questions are tangled together, and they go better separately:
1. **The deal.** It's signed. The real question is how to deliver it. That's a capacity and sequencing problem you can actually solve together: fourteen weeks, the extension clause, and the migration all on one table.
2. **How you two make decisions.** How to reach each other when something can't wait, who can commit engineering time, and how disagreements get handled. The engineering-channel post belongs here, since the team now needs one message from both of you.

If you lead with #1 and save #2 for later in the meeting, you're more likely to get through both.

**One step you could take**

Before Monday, or as your opening line, you could ask him something like:

*"I signed because I couldn't reach you and the offer was expiring. I know that put you in a bad spot. Before we talk about anything else, I want to understand what fourteen weeks looks like from your side. What would it take, and what would have to give?"*

That isn't conceding the signature was wrong. It opens with the question only he can answer, and his answer tells you a lot about whether this is a capacity problem, a process problem, or something bigger between you.

Whether to send it, say it, or neither is up to you. If you want, I can help you think through how you'd respond if he comes in hot.

I get why you're asking. After a week like this you want someone to say it.

Here's what I can say: you're right to feel exhausted, unsupported, and stung. You tried to reach him, you got better terms under pressure, and then you were hung up on and overruled in front of the team. Being upset about all of that is fair.

What I can't tell you, from one side, is whether signing without him was the right call or a line he reasonably expected you not to cross. I also can't tell you whether fourteen weeks is workable, or what's behind his pushback this year. Those depend on things only Tom can speak to, and I haven't heard him.

I don't say that to take his side. I say it because if you walk in Monday needing to be judged right, it'll be hard to hear him. If you walk in needing to understand what he's working with, you'll keep the ground you already have and maybe find out how much of this is fixable.
